name: Data Structures
author: Recurse
subject: cs
description: How arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, hash tables, trees, heaps and graphs work, what they cost, and when to use each.

lesson.intro: Every program stores data, and the structure you choose decides which operations are instant and which crawl. This pack covers the structures every developer uses: how each sits in memory, what its operations cost, and how to pick one for a feature or an interview.
objectives: State the cost of core operations on the common data structures
Explain O(1) amortized appends and O(1) average hash table lookups
Trace stack, queue, BST and heap operations by hand
Choose the structure that makes the most frequent operation cheap

sections.title: Arrays and dynamic arrays
sections.key: An array stores equal-size items side by side, so any index is one calculation away (O(1)); inserting or removing anywhere but the end shifts items, O(n).
sections.body:
Picture a hallway of equal-width lockers. Knowing where locker 0 is, you walk straight to locker 700. An **array** is the same: items of one size in one contiguous block, so `address = start + index × item_size`.

Reading `nums[700000]` is as fast as `nums[0]`: **random access**, O(1). The index is an offset, which is why it starts at 0.

The price comes when the shape changes. Inserting at the front slides every item right:

[[visual]]

Python's `list`, JavaScript's `Array`, Java's `ArrayList` and C++'s `vector` are **dynamic arrays**: they reserve more slots (the **capacity**) than they use (the **length**). When the spare slots run out, an append allocates a bigger block and copies everything: O(n). Growing by a constant **factor** keeps that rare, so append is **O(1) amortized**:

[[visual 2]]

[[visual 3]]

visual.title: `nums.insert(0, 7)`
visual.caption: Every existing item moved one slot: O(n). Deleting from the front slides them all back.

visual.title: Doubling through 9 appends
visual.caption: 15 copies for 9 appends, under 2n. CPython grows lists by about 12 percent and Java by 50; any factor above 1 works.

sections.tip: In JavaScript, `push` and `pop` work at the end of an array and are fast; `shift` and `unshift` work at the front and must move every other element.
sections.pitfall: Treating a Python list as a queue. `pop(0)` and `insert(0, x)` look innocent but shift every item, so draining a list from the front is O(n^2). Use `collections.deque`.

check.question: A dynamic array holds 1,000 items and its capacity is exactly 1,000. What does the next append cost?
choices: O(n): it allocates a bigger block and copies all 1,000 items first
O(1): appends never move existing items
O(log n): it only copies half of the items
Nothing: the append fails because the array is full
check.explanation: This append triggers a resize, so it copies all 1,000 items. The appends after it fill the new spare slots in O(1) each, which is why the amortized cost per append is still O(1).

sections.title: Linked lists
sections.key: A linked list chains nodes with pointers: reaching position i means following i pointers, O(n), but inserting or removing at a node you already hold is O(1).
sections.body:
In a scavenger hunt each clue says where the next one is. You cannot jump to clue 50, but adding a clue only means rewriting one pointer. That is a **linked list**: each **node** holds a value and a **pointer** to the next. The list remembers the **head**; the last node points to `None`.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

To walk a list, loop `while node:` and step with `node = node.next`. Testing `node.next` instead skips the last node and crashes on an empty list.

Lists rarely beat arrays in everyday code: scattered nodes are slow for CPU caches. They shine for constant changes at the ends or at held positions. Python's `deque` uses linked blocks, and an **LRU cache** pairs a hash map with a doubly linked list.

Reversal is the classic exercise. Save `nxt` before you flip each arrow:

[[code]]

visual.title: Insert 5 after the node holding 7
visual.caption: The list was 7 then 1. Inserting 5 changes two pointers: 7 now points to 5, and 5 points to 1. Nothing shifts.

rows: O(n): follow i pointers from the head
Insert or delete at the head
Insert after a node you hold
O(1); finding that node is the O(n) part
Unlink any node you hold (doubly linked)
O(1): each node also has a `prev` pointer
visual.caption: A **singly linked** node knows only its successor; a **doubly linked** one also knows its predecessor, at one extra pointer per node.

sections.code:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, value, next=None):
        self.value = value
        self.next = next

def reverse(head):
    prev, node = None, head
    while node:
        nxt = node.next   # 1. save the rest
        node.next = prev  # 2. flip arrow
        prev = node       # 3. step forward
        node = nxt
    return prev           # the new head

head = reverse(Node(1, Node(2, Node(3))))
print(head.value, head.next.value)  # 3 2
sections.deeper: An LRU (least recently used) cache makes get and put O(1) by pairing two structures. A hash map takes each key straight to its node in a doubly linked list kept in order of use. On every access the node is unlinked and moved to the front in O(1), and when the cache is full the node at the tail, the least recently used, is evicted in O(1).
sections.pitfall: Losing the rest of the list. If you overwrite `node.next` before saving it, every node after it becomes unreachable. Save the next pointer first, then rewire.

activity.title: Rewire the pointers
activity.prompt: Insert and delete a node to see that only neighboring arrows change. Then start the reversal and pick each line of code in order. Before every click, say which arrow is about to flip and why `nxt` must be saved first. Notice that each node is visited once: O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

check.question: You hold the head of a singly linked list of n nodes. What does it cost to read the value at position n // 2?
choices: O(log n)
O(n)
check.explanation: Nodes are scattered in memory, so there is no address arithmetic: you must follow about n/2 pointers from the head, which is O(n). O(1) access by index is the array's advantage, not the list's.

sections.title: Stacks and queues
sections.key: A stack is last in, first out: push and pop at the top. A queue is first in, first out: enqueue at the back, dequeue at the front.
sections.body:
Plates stack: you add and take at the top. A coffee line: you join at the back and leave from the front.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

A **stack** (**LIFO**) has `push`, `pop` and `peek`. A **queue** (**FIFO**) has `enqueue` and `dequeue`. Both are **abstract data types**: allowed operations built on an array or a linked list, each O(1) when it touches only the cheap end.

[[visual 3]]

Brackets close in reverse order of opening, so each closer must match the most recent unmatched opener: the top of a stack.

[[code]]

rows: `shift()` is O(n) on big arrays: keep a head index or use a queue class
undo, the back button, matching brackets, depth-first search, the **call stack**
print jobs, request backlogs, message queues, breadth-first search

sections.pitfall: Popping from an empty stack. Python's `[].pop()` raises IndexError, while JavaScript's `[].pop()` quietly returns undefined. Check the stack is not empty first, as `not stack` does above.

activity.title: LIFO and FIFO
activity.prompt: Start with the bracket walkthrough: push every opener, pop for every closer and check that the pair matches. Then switch to the queue and serve a few customers. Notice that the same items come out in opposite orders, and that each operation touches only one end.

check.question: You push 1, 2, 3 onto a stack and enqueue 1, 2, 3 into a queue. What do one pop and one dequeue return?
choices: Pop returns 1, dequeue returns 3
Both return 1
Both return 3
Pop returns 3, dequeue returns 1
check.explanation: A stack hands back the newest item (3), and a queue hands back the oldest (1). Mixing the two up is the most common slip, so tie them to plates and coffee lines.

sections.title: Hash tables
sections.key: A hash table turns each key into a bucket index, so insert, lookup and delete are O(1) on average; collisions are handled and resizing keeps buckets short.
sections.body:
A coat check with 100 hooks hangs each coat on hook (ticket number mod 100), so finding one is a single step. A **hash table** works the same way: a **hash function** turns the key into an integer, and modulo the bucket count picks the **bucket**.

[[visual]]

Two keys in one bucket is a **collision**. Both are stored, and lookups compare the actual keys:

[[visual 2]]

The **load factor** is entries divided by buckets. Past a threshold (0.75 in Java, about two-thirds in CPython) the table grows and reinserts every key, since buckets depend on the bucket count. That O(n) resize is rare, so inserts are O(1) amortized. If many keys collide, operations slide toward O(n).

Keys must be **hashable**: numbers, strings, tuples. A list could change after insertion and end up in the wrong bucket.

[[code]]

visual.title: Toy hash: character codes added up, mod 8
visual.caption: cat and act have the same letters, so the same sum: 312 mod 8 = 0. 6 entries in 8 buckets is a load factor of 0.75.

items.title: Chaining
points: Each bucket holds a small list of entries

items.title: Open addressing
points: A collision probes for another free slot

sections.code:
counts = {}
for word in "the cat and the hat".split():
    # counts[word] += 1 would raise KeyError
    counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1
print(counts["the"])   # 2

seen = set()
seen.add("cat")
print("cat" in seen)   # True, O(1) average

# {[1, 2]: "x"}  TypeError: unhashable list
d = {(1, 2): "x"}      # a tuple works
sections.tip: JavaScript `Map` and `Set` accept any value as a key. Plain objects work as maps too, but they turn every key into a string.
sections.pitfall: Using a mutable value as a key. Python raises `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'`, so convert to a tuple. In JavaScript, a Map compares arrays by identity, so a new `[1, 2]` never finds the old entry.

activity.title: Buckets and collisions
activity.prompt: Insert cat, then act. This toy hash adds up character codes, so anagrams always collide: watch act join cat's chain. Keep inserting until the load factor passes 0.75, then resize and notice that keys move to new buckets, because the bucket is the hash modulo the bucket count.

check.question: Why is looking up a key in a hash table O(1) on average?
choices: The table keeps its keys sorted and uses binary search
The table checks every bucket, but all at once
The key's hash points to the one bucket where it must be, so only that bucket is checked
Keys are stored in insertion order, so recent keys are found first
check.explanation: Hashing the key computes its bucket directly, and with a sensible load factor each bucket holds only a few entries. Sorted keys with binary search would be O(log n), and a table is not sorted at all.

sections.title: Trees and binary search trees
sections.key: In a binary search tree smaller keys go left and larger go right, so a search costs O(height): O(log n) if balanced, O(n) as a chain.
sections.body:
An org chart and your folders are **trees**: one **root**, and every other **node** has one **parent** and any number of **children**. Nodes without children are **leaves**; the **height** is the edges on the longest root-to-leaf path.

A **binary search tree (BST)** gives each node at most two children, with every key in the left subtree smaller and every key in the right subtree larger. Each comparison discards a whole subtree:

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

A BST's edge over a hash table is **order**: sorted listing, smallest or largest key, next key after x, every key in a range.

[[visual 3]]

[[code]]

visual.title: Insert 8, 3, 10, 1, 6, 14
visual.caption: Searching for 6: 6 < 8 go left, 6 > 3 go right, found in 3 comparisons.

items.title: Degenerate
points: Insert keys in sorted order: each goes right

visual.caption: **Self-balancing** trees (red-black, AVL) rotate nodes to keep height O(log n). Java's TreeMap and C++'s std::map are red-black trees.

visual.title: Depth-first traversals
rows: a BST's keys in sorted order: 1, 3, 6, 8, 10, 14
deleting a tree, totaling folder sizes: children finish first

sections.pitfall: Checking only direct children when validating a BST. The rule covers whole subtrees: a 9 anywhere in the left subtree of 8 breaks it, even if every parent and child pair looks fine.

activity.title: Search and traverse
activity.prompt: Search for 6 and count the comparisons: each one skips a whole subtree. Predict the in-order traversal before you run it, and check that it comes out sorted. Then rebuild the tree in sorted order and compare its height with the balanced order: same keys, very different search cost.

check.question: Keys 1 to 7 are inserted into an empty, non-balancing BST in increasing order. How many comparisons does a search for 7 take?
choices: 3, because a search halves the tree at each step
7, because every key became the right child of the one before
1, because 7 was the last key inserted
4, because 4 is the middle of 1 to 7
check.explanation: Sorted input builds a chain: 1 has right child 2, which has right child 3, and so on. The search compares with all seven keys. Only a balanced tree gives the log2(n) behavior, which is why self-balancing trees exist.

sections.title: Heaps and priority queues
sections.key: A binary min-heap keeps the smallest item at the root of a complete tree stored in an array: peek is O(1), push and pop are O(log n).
sections.body:
An emergency room treats the most urgent patient next, not the earliest. A **priority queue** does that: insert items with priorities, always remove the highest priority.

The usual implementation is a **binary heap**. In a **min-heap** every parent is at most its children. Siblings are unordered and the tree is not sorted: only the root is promised to be the minimum.

A heap is a **complete** tree (every level full except the last, filled from the left), so it fits in a plain array with no pointers:

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

[[visual 3]]

Heaps make top-k cheap: to keep the 10 largest values of a stream, hold a min-heap of 10 and replace its smallest when a bigger value arrives. O(n log k) time, O(k) memory.

Python's `heapq` is a min-heap on a list; for a max-heap, push negated values.

[[code]]

visual.title: The same heap as an array
visual.caption: Children of index i sit at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2; the parent of i is at (i - 1) // 2.

rows: append at the end, then **sift up**: swap with the parent while smaller
take the root, move the last item there, then **sift down** past the smaller child
turn a whole list into a heap

sections.code:
import heapq

tasks = []  # (priority, task)
heapq.heappush(tasks, (2, "write tests"))
heapq.heappush(tasks, (1, "fix prod bug"))
heapq.heappush(tasks, (3, "update docs"))
print(tasks[0])              # peek: O(1)
print(heapq.heappop(tasks))  # O(log n)
# (1, 'fix prod bug') both times

nums = [5, 1, 9, 3, 7]
heapq.heapify(nums)   # O(n)
print(nums[0])        # 1, the minimum
sections.tip: When two priorities tie, Python compares the next item in the tuple. If tasks cannot be compared, add a counter as a tiebreaker: `(priority, count, task)`.
sections.pitfall: Expecting a heap to be sorted. Only `heap[0]` is guaranteed; `heap[1]` is not necessarily the second smallest. To get items in order, pop them one at a time.

check.question: In an array-based heap, where are the children of the node at index 3?
choices: Indexes 4 and 5
Indexes 6 and 7
Indexes 1 and 2
Indexes 7 and 8
check.explanation: Children of i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, so 2 × 3 + 1 = 7 and 2 × 3 + 2 = 8. Indexes 1 and 2 are the children of the root, index 0.

sections.title: Graphs
sections.key: A graph is vertices plus edges; store it as an adjacency list (O(V + E) memory) unless it is dense or you constantly check single edges.
sections.body:
Airline routes, friendships, web links and package dependencies share one shape: things and connections. That is a **graph**, a set of **vertices** and the **edges** between them. Linked lists and trees are special cases.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

Most real graphs are **sparse**: each vertex connects to a few others. So the default is an **adjacency list**, in Python a dict of lists:

[[visual 3]]

[[code]]

visual.title: Edges A-B, A-C, B-D, C-D, D-E
Graph flavors
rows: an edge A to B goes one way: A to B, not necessarily back
some path leads back to its start
task dependencies, build systems, course prerequisites

items.title: Adjacency list
points: Each vertex maps to its neighbors
Neighbors of v: O(degree of v)

items.title: Adjacency matrix
points: A V × V grid: cell [u][v] says if the edge exists
Check one edge: O(1); list neighbors: O(V)
For dense graphs or constant edge checks

sections.code:
graph = {
    "A": ["B", "C"],
    "B": ["A", "D"],
    "C": ["A", "D"],
    "D": ["B", "C", "E"],
    "E": ["D"],
}
print(graph["D"])   # ['B', 'C', 'E']

# Undirected: each edge is listed twice
listed = sum(len(n) for n in graph.values())
print(listed // 2)  # 5 edges
sections.deeper: Most graph problems, from shortest paths to cycle detection to ordering tasks by their dependencies, are traversals over an adjacency list with breadth-first or depth-first search, which the algorithms pack covers. The matrix wins only when most pairs of vertices are connected, or when the code checks "is there an edge from u to v?" far more often than it lists neighbors.
sections.pitfall: Adding an undirected edge in only one direction. If A lists B but B does not list A, a search starting at B never finds A. Append every undirected edge to both endpoints' lists.

check.question: A social network has 10 million users with about 200 friends each. How should the friendship graph be stored?
choices: As an adjacency list: a matrix would need 10^14 cells that are almost all empty
As an adjacency matrix: checking one friendship is O(1)
As one flat list of all users, scanned for each query
As a binary search tree keyed by user name
check.explanation: The graph is sparse: about a billion edges against 10^14 possible pairs. An adjacency list stores only the edges that exist. The matrix's O(1) edge check is not worth petabytes of zeros.

sections.title: Choosing the right structure
sections.key: Start from the operation your code performs most often, pick the structure that makes it cheap, and say the reason out loud.
sections.body:
Many interview problems and slow features come down to one question: which structure makes the expensive operation cheap?

[[visual]]

Real solutions combine structures. An LRU cache is a hash map plus a doubly linked list; Dijkstra's algorithm runs a heap over a graph; a list plus a "seen" set keeps order and fast membership.

In an interview, say the choice and the reason: "I'll keep a set of values I've seen, so each check is O(1) and the pass is O(n) instead of O(n^2)." Know these costs cold:

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: Decision guide
rows: Items by position, mostly adding at the end
"Have I seen this?" or "value for this key?"
The smallest or largest, again and again, as items arrive
**balanced BST** (or a sorted array if data rarely changes)
Constant adds and removes at both ends

visual.title: Operation costs
visual.caption: Hash tables degrade to O(n) when many keys collide.

sections.pitfall: Reaching for a fancy structure before you need one. For 50 items, a list is fine. Big-O differences matter when n is large or the operation sits inside a loop.

check.question: Each of 1 million incoming emails must be checked against a blocklist of 50,000 addresses. Which structure should hold the blocklist for the cheapest lookups?
choices: A list, scanned for each email
A hash set
A min-heap of addresses
A stack of addresses
check.explanation: A hash set answers each membership check in O(1) on average, so the whole job is about 1 million steps. Scanning a list costs up to 50,000 comparisons per email, and a heap only knows its smallest item.

keyTerms.definition: An array that keeps spare capacity and grows by a constant factor when full, giving O(1) amortized appends. Python's list and JavaScript's Array.
The average cost per operation over a long sequence, where rare expensive steps (like a resize) are spread across many cheap ones.
A chain of nodes, each holding a value and a pointer to the next node. O(1) inserts at a known node, O(n) access by index.
A last in, first out (LIFO) collection with push, pop and peek at one end.
A first in, first out (FIFO) collection: add at the back, remove from the front. Use collections.deque in Python.
A structure that hashes each key to a bucket index, giving O(1) average insert, lookup and delete. Python's dict and set.
Two different keys landing in the same bucket. Handled by chaining or open addressing, comparing real keys on lookup.
Entries divided by buckets. When it passes a threshold, the hash table resizes and rehashes every key.
A binary tree where left subtrees hold smaller keys and right subtrees larger ones. O(h) operations; O(log n) when balanced.
A complete binary tree, stored in an array, where each parent is no larger than its children (min-heap). O(1) peek, O(log n) push and pop.
A graph representation mapping each vertex to its neighbors. O(V + E) memory; the default for sparse graphs.

summary: Arrays: O(1) access by index, O(n) inserts except at the end; appends are O(1) amortized.
Linked lists: O(n) to reach an index, O(1) to insert or remove at a node you hold.
Stacks are LIFO and queues FIFO: in Python, a list for a stack and a deque for a queue.
Hash tables give O(1) average lookups, balanced BSTs O(log n) plus order, heaps the minimum in O(1).
Graphs are vertices plus edges, usually adjacency lists in O(V + E) memory.
Pick the structure by the most frequent operation, and say why out loud.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend who has never programmed why looking a name up in a hash map is fast, why appending to a dynamic array is cheap on average even though it sometimes copies everything, and how you would choose between a list, a set and a heap for a job.

questions.question: Which operation on a Python list of n items is O(n)?
choices: nums[500]
nums.append(x)
nums.insert(0, x)
len(nums)
questions.explanation: Inserting at index 0 shifts every existing item one slot right, so the work grows with n. Indexing and len are O(1), and append writes into spare capacity at the end, which is O(1) amortized.

questions.question: You already hold a reference to a node in the middle of a singly linked list. What does it cost to insert a new node right after it?
choices: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
questions.explanation: Only two references change: the new node points to the old next node, and the current node points to the new one. The O(n) cost people expect is for finding the position by walking from the head, which has already been done here.

questions.question: This function should return the number of nodes in a linked list. What is wrong?
questions.code:
def length(head):
    count = 0
    node = head
    while node.next:
        count += 1
        node = node.next
    return count
choices: count should start at 1 instead of 0
The loop tests node.next instead of node, so it skips the last node and crashes on an empty list
node = node.next should come before count += 1
A linked list cannot be walked with a while loop
questions.explanation: With `while node.next`, the loop stops while standing on the last node without counting it, so a 3-node list returns 2. On an empty list head is None, and None.next raises AttributeError. `while node:` fixes both. Starting count at 1 fixes non-empty lists but still crashes on an empty one.

questions.question: What does this code print?
questions.code:
stack = []
for x in [1, 2, 3]:
    stack.append(x)
stack.pop()
stack.append(4)
print(stack.pop() + stack.pop())
questions.explanation: After pushing 1, 2 and 3 the stack is [1, 2, 3]. pop() removes 3, then 4 is pushed: [1, 2, 4]. The next two pops return 4 and then 2, so it prints 6. A queue would have removed 1 first.

questions.question: Fill the blank to remove and return the item that joined the queue first.
questions.code:
from collections import deque

queue = deque(["a", "b", "c"])
first = queue._____()
print(first)  # a
choices: pop
shift
dequeue
popleft
questions.explanation: popleft removes from the front of a deque in O(1), giving first in, first out order. pop removes from the right end and would return 'c'. shift and dequeue are names from other languages; deque has neither method.

questions.question: This bracket checker returns False for "([])", which is balanced. What is the bug?
choices: ch in "([" should be ch in pairs
It should return True instead of not stack
stack.pop(0) takes the oldest opener; stack.pop() would take the most recent one
The pairs dict maps closers to openers backwards
questions.explanation: Brackets close in the reverse order they opened, which is exactly last in, first out. When ']' arrives, its partner is the newest opener, '['. pop(0) takes '(' from the bottom instead. Returning `not stack` is correct: it rejects text that leaves an opener unclosed.

questions.question: Your program receives 100,000 IDs and must report each one it has seen before. Which type should seen be?
choices: list
set
tuple
deque
questions.explanation: `id in seen` is O(1) on average for a set, so the whole job is about O(n). For a list or a deque each check scans the items, making the job O(n^2). A tuple cannot even be added to.

questions.question: What is the average time complexity of `key in d` for a Python dict with n keys? Answer in Big-O notation.
questions.explanation: The key's hash points straight to the slot where it would be, so the cost does not grow with n. It only becomes O(n) in the rare worst case where many keys collide.

questions.question: This should count how often each word appears. What goes wrong?
choices: counts[word] += 1 raises KeyError the first time a word is seen
Dict keys cannot be strings
It prints {'red': 1, 'blue': 1} because dicts ignore repeats
counts must be created with dict() instead of {}
questions.explanation: `+=` reads counts[word] before writing it, and reading a missing key raises KeyError. Use `counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1` or collections.Counter. {} and dict() create the same empty dict.

questions.question: Two different keys hash to the same slot in a hash map. What happens?
choices: The second key silently replaces the first
Python raises a KeyError on insert
The map is rebuilt so that no collisions can happen again
Both are stored, and lookups compare keys to find the right one
questions.explanation: Collisions are normal. The table keeps both entries, by probing for another slot or chaining, and compares the actual keys during lookup. Only an equal key replaces a value; a different key with the same hash never overwrites it.

questions.question: You insert 8, 3, 10, 1, 6 into an empty BST, in that order. What does an in-order traversal return?
questions.explanation: In-order visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree, which in a BST always yields the keys in sorted order. [8, 3, 1, 6, 10] is the pre-order (node first) and [1, 6, 3, 10, 8] is the post-order (node last).

questions.question: Fill the blank so this BST search goes the right way at each node.
questions.explanation: Smaller keys live in the left subtree, so when key < node.key the search must go left. With > the search turns the wrong way at every node and misses keys that are in the tree.

questions.question: A min-heap holds n items. What is the time complexity of heapq.heappop? Answer in Big-O notation.
questions.explanation: Popping removes the root, moves the last item to the top and sifts it down one level at a time. A heap is a complete binary tree about log2(n) levels deep, so this is O(log n). Only peeking at heap[0] is O(1).

questions.question: After heapq.heapify(nums) on a list of distinct numbers, which statement is always true?
choices: nums is sorted in ascending order
nums[1] is the second smallest item
nums[-1] is the largest item
nums[0] is the smallest item
questions.explanation: A min-heap only promises that each parent is less than or equal to its children, which puts the minimum at index 0. The rest is only partly ordered: the second smallest may be at index 1 or 2, and the list is usually not sorted. heapify([1, 5, 2]) leaves it as [1, 5, 2].

questions.question: A graph has V vertices and E edges. In Big-O, how much memory does an adjacency list need?
questions.explanation: It stores one entry per vertex plus one list item per edge (two for an undirected edge, which is still O(E)). An adjacency matrix needs O(V^2) no matter how few edges there are.

questions.question: A server must always run the waiting job with the highest priority next, while new jobs keep arriving. Which structure fits best?
choices: A queue (deque)
A list sorted again after each insert
A heap
A set
questions.explanation: A heap gives the top-priority item in O(1) and supports insert and remove in O(log n). Keeping a list sorted costs at least O(n) per insert, and a plain queue serves jobs by arrival time, not priority.

questions.question: When would you pick an adjacency matrix instead of an adjacency list?
questions.answer: When the graph is dense (most pairs of vertices are connected) or when you must check whether a specific edge exists very often. The matrix answers that in O(1) but always costs O(V^2) memory.
questions.explanation: For sparse graphs, which most real graphs are, the O(V^2) matrix is mostly zeros, so adjacency lists are the default.

questions.question: An array of 4-byte integers starts at memory address 1000. At what address does the element at index 5 start?
questions.explanation: address = start + index × size = 1000 + 5 × 4 = 1020. Index 0 starts at 1000 itself, which is why indexes count from 0: the index is an offset from the start, not a position number.

questions.question: Which of these Python list operations are O(1)? Count amortized O(1) as O(1). Select all that apply.
choices: nums[i] = x
nums.append(x)
nums.pop()
nums.pop(0)
nums.insert(len(nums) // 2, x)
len(nums)
questions.explanation: Assigning by index, appending, popping from the end and len all leave the other items where they are. pop(0) shifts every remaining item left, and inserting in the middle shifts the back half right, so both are O(n).

questions.question: Which operation is O(1) on a singly linked list (you hold the head) but O(n) on an array?
choices: Reading the item at index n // 2
Finding the largest value
Searching for a given value
Inserting a new item at the front
questions.explanation: A new head node just points at the old head: one pointer change. An array must shift all n items right to free index 0. Reading by index is the reverse (O(1) for the array, O(n) for the list), and searching or finding the maximum is O(n) for both.

questions.question: Which of these are naturally handled with a stack? Select all that apply.
choices: Undo in a text editor
Checking that brackets are balanced
Serving print jobs in the order they arrived
Tracking which functions are currently running
Exploring a graph level by level (BFS)
questions.explanation: Undo, bracket matching and the call stack all need the most recent unfinished item first, which is LIFO. Print jobs and breadth-first search need the oldest item first, which is a queue.

questions.question: This JavaScript loop drains a queue of 200,000 jobs but takes many seconds. What is the problem?
choices: shift() removes index 0, so every remaining element moves down one slot; the loop is O(n^2)
push() copies the whole array each time, so filling the queue is O(n^2)
queue.length counts the elements one by one on every check
Objects are slower to remove than numbers, so the queue should hold ids
questions.explanation: On a large array, removing the first element shifts all the others down, an O(n) step repeated n times. Keep a head index that moves forward instead, or use a real queue. push is amortized O(1), and length is a stored property, not a count.

questions.question: Match each need with the structure that fits it best.

pairs.left: Check whether a username is already taken
Always handle the task with the earliest deadline next
Record which cities have direct flights between them
Answer support tickets in the order they arrived

questions.explanation: Most recent first is LIFO (stack); membership is a hash set; repeatedly taking the minimum is a heap; connections between things are a graph; first come, first served is FIFO (queue).

questions.question: Why does Python reject {[1, 2]: "x"} with TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'?
choices: Lists are too large to hash quickly
Dict keys must be strings or numbers
A list could change after insertion, so its hash would no longer match the bucket it was stored in
Lists are ordered, and dict keys must be unordered
questions.explanation: A key's bucket is chosen from its hash when it is inserted. If the key could be modified, its hash would change and lookups would search the wrong bucket. Tuples of hashable values work fine as keys, so 'strings or numbers only' is too strict.

questions.question: A balanced BST holds about 1,000,000 keys. Roughly how many comparisons does a search need in the worst case?
questions.explanation: Each comparison discards a whole subtree, about half of what is left, so the worst case is about log2(1,000,000), roughly 20 levels. A chain-shaped tree built from sorted input could need a million comparisons instead.

questions.question: Put the keys in the order a pre-order traversal visits them.
questions.explanation: Pre-order visits the node first, then its whole left subtree, then its right subtree: 8, then the subtree under 3 (3, 1, 6), then the subtree under 10 (10, 14). In-order would give the sorted 1, 3, 6, 8, 10, 14.

questions.question: In an array-based heap, the children of index i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2. What is the index of the parent of the node at index 9?
questions.explanation: The parent is at (i - 1) // 2 = (9 - 1) // 2 = 4. Check it the other way: the children of 4 are 2 × 4 + 1 = 9 and 2 × 4 + 2 = 10.

questions.question: heapq only provides a min-heap. Fill the blank so this prints the largest score first.
questions.code:
import heapq

heap = []
for score in [40, 95, 70]:
    heapq.heappush(heap, _____)
print(-heapq.heappop(heap))   # 95
choices: score
-score
abs(score)
(score, -1)
questions.explanation: Negating turns the largest score into the smallest number, so it sits at the root of the min-heap, and negating again on the way out restores it. Pushing score itself would pop 40 first, and the final minus sign would print -40.

questions.question: How many edges does this undirected graph have?
questions.explanation: The lists hold 2 + 2 + 3 + 1 = 8 entries, and in an undirected graph every edge appears twice, once at each end. That gives 8 / 2 = 4 edges: A-B, A-C, B-C and C-D.

questions.question: A program inserts keys constantly, looks keys up, lists all keys in sorted order and often asks for every key between 100 and 200. Which structure fits best?
choices: A hash map
A min-heap
A plain array, sorted again after each insert
A balanced binary search tree
questions.explanation: A balanced BST does lookups, inserts and deletes in O(log n) and keeps keys in order, so sorted listing and range queries come naturally (Java's TreeMap, C++'s std::map). A hash map has no order, a heap only knows its minimum, and re-sorting an array after every insert is expensive.

questions.question: Why can an array read nums[700000] as fast as nums[0]?
choices: The CPU keeps every element of every array in its cache
The array is searched with binary search, which is nearly instant
The element's address is computed directly: start + index × item size
Arrays scan from both ends at once, halving the work
questions.explanation: Elements sit side by side and are the same size, so one multiplication and one addition give any element's address and no scanning happens. (A Python list stores same-size references to its objects, so the same arithmetic applies.)

questions.question: In a directed graph, what does an edge from A to B mean?
choices: A and B are connected in both directions
You can go from A to B, but not necessarily from B to A
B must always be visited before A
A and B have the same weight
questions.explanation: Directed edges are one-way, like following someone who does not follow you back. The two-way version is an undirected edge. Some problems use direction to mean an ordering, but the edge itself only says A connects to B.

questions.question: A hash table holds 12 entries in 16 buckets. What is its load factor?
questions.explanation: Load factor = entries / buckets = 12 / 16 = 0.75, exactly where Java's HashMap resizes. The higher the load factor, the more collisions and the longer each lookup takes.

questions.question: How does an LRU (least recently used) cache make both get and put O(1)?
questions.answer: It pairs a hash map from each key to a node in a doubly linked list kept in order of use. The map finds a node in O(1), the node is unlinked and moved to the front in O(1), and when the cache is full the node at the tail (least recently used) is evicted in O(1).
questions.explanation: Neither structure works alone: a list alone needs O(n) to find a key, and a map alone has no notion of recency. The prev pointers of the doubly linked list let a node be unlinked without searching for the node before it.
